blocks.text: Recycling is an important part of waste management, conservation of resources and energy saving. Yet modern materials face severe technical, economic and environmental limits to recycling and reuse, and with more complex synthetic products, toxicity and sustainable disposal have become a rising concern.

Recycling reduces the solid waste going to landfills and preserves limited natural resources such as metals, oil and timber. It also saves energy: recycling aluminium uses 95 percent less energy than extracting aluminium from its raw ore.

items: Separation: most products (for example mobile phones and laptops) are made of mixed materials that are not easily separated, such as plastic coatings on metals or multi-layered packaging films.

Expensive reprocessing: sorting, cleaning and other steps cost money, and reprocessing plastics and electronics needs a lot of energy, which is uneconomical when the material is available elsewhere at a lower price.

Contamination: recycled metals and plastics can be contaminated by dyes, chemicals or biological materials, which lowers their quality and safety; contaminated plastic cannot be recycled for food-grade use.

blocks.caption: Table 31.3 Principles and methods of recycling some important materials
rows: Sorting, cleaning, melting and re-forming the plastic; limited by contamination and degradation of the polymer chains
Breaking the polymer chains into the original monomers or simpler chemicals using heat, solvents or catalysts; gives purer reactants
Melting and refining to remove impurities; needs significant energy, but much less than primary production
Chemical and mechanical separation of fibres; the pulp is treated with chemicals such as NaOH or Na2CO3 to remove inks and dyes
Cleaning, crushing and melting scrap glass (cullet) to form new glass; chemically simpler, as glass is a non-crystalline solid

blocks.alt: Two flow charts for plastics. Mechanical recycling: collect and sort, clean, melt, re-form into new items; the chains degrade and contamination limits it. Chemical recycling: polymer chains are broken down with heat, solvents or catalysts into monomers or simple chemicals, which make new polymer. Below: metals are melted and refined (recycled aluminium needs about 95% less energy), paper is pulped and de-inked with NaOH or Na2CO3, and glass cullet is cleaned, crushed and melted.
blocks.caption: Recycling routes (original diagram after Table 31.3).
blocks.long_description: Mechanical recycling reuses the polymer as it is, so its quality falls each time. Chemical recycling breaks the polymer back to monomers, so the new polymer can be as good as the original.

blocks.prompt: Name two types of hazards caused by toxic materials.
blocks.explanation: Any two of: health hazards, physical hazards and environmental hazards.

blocks.prompt: Which methods would you use to recycle (i) empty metal food cans, (ii) empty glass bottles, (iii) shopping bags and toys?
blocks.explanation: (i) Thermal and chemical refining: melting and refining the metal. (ii) Cullet preparation and melting. (iii) These are plastics: mechanical recycling (sort, clean, melt, re-form) or chemical recycling (depolymerisation).

blocks.prompt: How do heavy metals enter the food chain?
blocks.explanation: From discarded electronics, batteries and lights they leach into soil and groundwater; plants and aquatic organisms such as fish take them up, and animals and humans eat these.

blocks.prompt: How does recycling help conserve natural resources?
blocks.explanation: Recycled metals, plastics (from oil) and paper (from timber) replace new raw materials, so fewer resources are extracted; it also saves energy (aluminium recycling uses 95% less) and reduces landfill waste.

items: Recycling saves resources and energy (Al: 95% less energy).
Plastics: mechanical or chemical; metals: refining; paper: pulping, de-inking; glass: cullet.
